title: Feedback That Changes What People Do

audience.who: corporate employees who give feedback to peers or reports
audience.knows: feedback matters, but often says something vague like 'be more proactive' and hopes it lands
audience.cares_about: getting a real change in how a colleague works without damaging the relationship

outcome: After watching, the viewer can take one piece of feedback they were about to give and rewrite it so it names a specific observed behaviour, its effect, and a clear next step the other person can try.
through_line: Feedback feels kind when it soothes, but it only works when it hands the other person something they can see and do differently.

arc_plan.what: Open on a manager who gives a warm, vague 'great job, just be a bit more engaged' to a colleague; the glow fades and nothing changes by the next meeting.
Promise the viewer a way to turn the same remark into feedback the colleague can act on, using the same running scene.
Connect the viewer's own recent feedback moments to the opening scene: they liked how it felt to say, but did anyone do anything different?
Rework the opening remark step by step: swap the label for a specific observed behaviour, add its effect on the team, then a concrete next step agreed together. Each part is named after it appears.
Give the viewer two versions of a new remark and have them pick which one a colleague could act on and say why, before the answer is shown.
Invite the viewer to rewrite one real piece of upcoming feedback in the three parts, and choose when to deliver it.
Return to the opening meeting with the reworked feedback: the colleague responds with a concrete change, and the relationship is intact.

must_cover.what: Why vague or purely pleasant feedback feels good but rarely changes what people do
Describe observable behaviour, not personality or labels
State the effect of the behaviour on the work or team
Agree a specific next step the person can try
Make feedback timely and keep it a two-way conversation

must_avoid: Statistics or research figures without a source
Invented statements attributed to real people or studies
Opening with a dictionary-style explanation or agenda slide
Lecturing tone; speak as a capable colleague
Treating kind and effective as opposites
Several one-off examples instead of one running scene
example_posture: One running workplace scene (a team meeting and one colleague) that returns throughout; the vague remark is rewritten in front of the viewer. Examples are illustrative and realistic, never presented as real cases.
visual_direction: Story-cartoon look with a person in a situation: two colleagues in a meeting room. A remark that visibly sharpens from a fuzzy cloud into specific parts, a before and after of the same scene, and one board built up by additions. One loud thing on screen at a time.
voice_note: Mentor: warm, plain and direct, a colleague who has made this mistake herself. Encouraging without gushing, no teacher tone.
open_questions: Which feedback model, if any, should the knowledge sheet anchor the three parts to?
Does the audience mostly give feedback to peers or to direct reports?
